name: Arabes Choa (Garoua)
parler: Shuwa Arabic; fulfulde as the language of daily use
overview: A minority in Garoua, the Shuwa Arabs live among the Fali, Guiziga, Bata and Fulani, with whom they share Fulfulde. Arriving three centuries ago from Ouaddaï (Abéché, Chad) via Mora, they have made their three-hundred-year-old mosque and the chiefdom their places of memory. Small-scale trade, tontines and catering occupy the women; milk and the sorghum ball are at the heart of the cuisine.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group, integrated with the Fali, Guiziga, Bata and Fulani; all speak Fulfulde.
Shuwa Arabic is spoken in Logone-et-Chari, Diamaré, Mayo-Danay, Vina and Bénoué.
Mixed group; exogamous marriages are in the majority, especially among men.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The group has occupied these lands for three centuries.
Having come from the Ouaddaï (Abéché, Chad), they stayed at Mora (Mayo-Sava) and keep ties with these places.
The three-hundred-year-old mosque and the chiefdom are the group's symbolic places.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kingship and land ownership organise society; decisions are made by common agreement, but the chief's word prevails.
All, women, children and adults, interact freely; the in-laws keep a reserve made of humility.
Blacksmiths and mourners form hereditary groups.
All ethnic groups are represented at the court, which has made it possible to bury antagonisms.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family.
The boy becomes a man at puberty, through circumcision; the girl on reaching adulthood. People marry at around 25 for men, 18 for women.
Steps: request and engagement, bride price, religious marriage, then civil marriage.
The bride price, in goods or money, is negotiated between the future spouses; it proves the suitor's seriousness, honesty and faith.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship: the mosque is the place of worship, the chiefdom the place of memory.
Birth is a joy; death, a sorrow. The dead are honoured through prayer.
Duties: the man educates, feeds, instructs and clothes his family; the wife respects her husband; the children respect their parents.
Serious offences: adultery, crime, association (idolatry).

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Women engage in petty trade (fritters, baobab fruit, jujubes), run tontines and keep small eating-houses.
The land belongs to whoever puts it to productive use; it is accessed by inheritance, purchase or gift.
Ancestral crafts: dried skins of the Tabaski sheep, made into prayer mats and rugs, on which Quranic teachers also sit.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men: gandoura, djellaba, but also suits; women: wrapper, hijab, skirts and blouses, and for young people T-shirts and jeans.
Traditional medicine is well established: cheaper and more accessible.
Beauty: the tall, strong man; the full-figured woman with beautiful hair.
Courtship: gifts, elegance, culinary talent, and good upbringing (respect, obedience).

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Music: algaita (chiefdom orchestra), mbaylaou (weddings), gousna (major events), massera (harvests); instruments: flute, trumpet, tam-tam.
The algaita is danced at the festivals of the sheep and of Ramadan, the mbaylaou at weddings, the gourna at the cockerel festival, the massera at the harvest festival.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The group is distinguished by its social cohesion and good understanding with its neighbours.

sections.title: The names
items: The child receives his name one week after birth, during a Muslim ceremony.
A name may be changed once, if the child is often ill, on the advice of a healer.
A child named after a parent is nicknamed Baba or Abba (for the father), Oummi, Dada or Inna (for the mother).
The founder, Mansour, is nicknamed Heurso, “brave warrior” in Fulfulde.

lessons.title: Who are the Arabes Choa (Garoua)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Arabes Choa (Garoua) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: E the other side of the marsh

lessons.competence: Introduce the Arabes Choa (Garoua) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Arabes Choa (Garoua) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Arabes Choa (Garoua) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Arabes Choa (Garoua) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Arabes Choa (Garoua) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Minority group, integrated with the Fali, Guiziga, Bata and Fulani; all speak Fulfulde. • Shuwa Arabic is spoken in Logone-et-Chari, Diamaré, Mayo-Danay, Vina and Bénoué. • Mixed group; exogamous marriages are in the majority, especially among men. • The group has occupied these lands for three centuries. • Coming from Ouaddaï (Abéché, Chad), they stayed in Mora (Mayo-Sava) and keep ties with these places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A minority in Garoua, the Shuwa Arabs live among the Fali, Guiziga, Bata and Fulani, with whom they share Fulfulde. Arriving three centuries ago from Ouaddaï (Abéché, Chad) via Mora, they have made their three-hundred-year-old mosque and the chiefdom their places of memory. Small-scale trade, tontines and catering occupy the women; milk and the sorghum ball are at the heart of the cuisine.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Arabes Choa (Garoua) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

objectives: Linking food to the living environment

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Arabes Choa (Garoua), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.

lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Arabes Choa (Garoua), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Arabes Choa (Garoua).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: sorghum balls with baobab leaf sauce, fresh milk with couscous. • Drinks: tchoura (spiced curdled milk), lemon juice, sorrel juice, bil-bil. • Women run small businesses (fritters, baobab fruit, jujubes), run tontines and keep small eating houses. • The land belongs to whoever develops it; it is acquired by inheritance, purchase or gift.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Arabes Choa (Garoua) eat mainly sorghum balls and baobab leaf sauce, fresh milk with couscous. Traditional drinks: spiced curdled milk, lemon juice, sorrel juice. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Arabes Choa (Garoua)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Arabes Choa (Garoua), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Arabes Choa (Garoua). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Arabes Choa (Garoua), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Arabes Choa (Garoua). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Women run small businesses (fritters, baobab fruit, jujubes), run tontines and keep small eating houses. • The land belongs to whoever develops it; it is acquired by inheritance, purchase or gift. • Ancestral crafts: dried skins of the Tabaski sheep, made into mats and prayer rugs, on which Koranic teachers also sit.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Women engage in petty trade (fritters, baobab fruit, jujubes), run tontines and keep small eating-houses. The land belongs to whoever develops it; it is acquired through inheritance, purchase or gift.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Arabes Choa (Garoua)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Arabes Choa (Garoua)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Arabes Choa (Garoua), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Arabes Choa (Garoua). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Arabes Choa (Garoua), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Arabes Choa (Garoua). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No ancestor worship: the mosque is the place of worship, the chiefdom the place of memory. • Birth is a joy; death, a sorrow. The dead are honoured through prayer. • Duties: the man educates, feeds, instructs and clothes his family; the woman respects her husband; children respect their parents. • Serious offences: adultery, crime, association (idolatry).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestor worship: the mosque is the place of worship, the chiefdom the place of memory. Birth is a joy; death, a sadness. The dead are honoured through prayer.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Arabes Choa (Garoua) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: No ancestor worship: the mosque is the place of worship, the chiefdom the place of memory. Birth is a joy; death, a sadness. The dead are honoured through prayer.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Arabe choa
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Arabes Choa (Garoua) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Arabes Choa (Garoua) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Arabes Choa (Garoua) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Arabes Choa (Garoua) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Shuwa Arabic. • Greeting formulae: sannou = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Awali djam nâ = morning greeting (one person); Ein mbali djamna = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Go’o, Didi, Tati, Naye, Djoye. • The founder, Mansour, is nicknamed Heurso, “brave warrior” in Fulfulde. • The group is distinguished by its social cohesion and good relations with its neighbours.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Choa Arabic are the first steps towards communicating with the Arabes Choa (Garoua). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Shuwa Arabic.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Choa Arabic are the first steps towards communicating with the Arabes Choa (Garoua). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
